name: QC Fails Every GPT Test
subject: quantum-computing
subjectTitle: A Skeptic's Guide to Quantum Computing

lesson.title: Running the Same Checklist on Quantum Computers
lesson.summary: Applying the same three general purpose technology tests that AI clears easily to quantum computing produces a failing grade on all three, not because the physics is fake but because the class of problems it actually helps with is narrow and the path to broad economic impact is currently missing.
lesson.body:
The previous chapter walked through the three tests economists use to identify a general purpose technology: broad applicability across sectors, sustained improvement over time, and the capacity to enable genuinely new complementary innovations. Artificial intelligence passed all three without much strain. Running quantum computing through the same checklist is a useful exercise precisely because it treats quantum computing fairly, on the criteria that actually distinguish transformative technologies from merely interesting ones, rather than on vibes or press coverage.

Broad applicability fails first and most clearly. Quantum computers offer a real, mathematically demonstrated advantage for a narrow and mathematically specific set of problems: certain factoring and cryptographic problems, simulating other quantum systems, and some optimization and sampling tasks. They offer no benefit, and often a severe practical disadvantage, for the overwhelming majority of what computers actually do: serving web pages, running spreadsheets, streaming video, managing databases, and even training most of today's machine learning models. This is narrow problem applicability in a strict sense, not a temporary limitation of early hardware but a structural feature of what quantum mechanics can and cannot speed up.

The improve-over-time test produces a genuinely ambiguous answer. Qubit counts and coherence times have risen over the past two decades, and that is real engineering progress worth taking seriously. But there is nothing resembling a smooth, broadly applicable curve of falling cost per unit of useful work, the kind AI can point to. The field is still commonly described as being in the noisy intermediate-scale quantum era, meaning error rates remain high enough to limit which problems can be solved reliably, and the error correction overhead required for genuinely fault-tolerant machines remains a major open engineering question rather than a solved one.

The third test, enabling new complementary innovations, is where the gap with AI is starkest. Unlike artificial intelligence, where entire new product categories and workflows have visibly formed on top of the underlying capability, most of today's commercial quantum computing activity consists of hardware makers and cloud access providers selling capability itself, not a wave of downstream applications delivering measured value from quantum advantage. There is not yet a quantum equivalent of the coding assistant or the recommendation engine, a genuinely new thing that exists because of the technology and that ordinary users or businesses now depend on.

It is worth being precise about what this failing grade does and does not mean. It does not mean quantum computing is fake, or that it will never matter, general purpose technology status is not necessarily permanent or predetermined, and a technology can in principle mature into passing these tests later just as it can fail to. What it does mean is that quantum computing, as it stands today, is not on the same track as artificial intelligence or the historical general purpose technologies, and the reason traces specifically to narrow problem applicability, which the next chapter examines in concrete detail.
